headline: AI×HPC Weekly Watch (2026-11-09): An AI-Native Lab Runs 11,000+ Hardware Steps, a 614-PF Supercomputer Goes Live, and Open Weights Get a Safety Gate
text: Summary: In the week of November 2-8, four threads of AI×HPC advanced at once. First, AI-native science moved from 'assistant tooling' to end-to-end execution: a Shanghai Jiao Tong University team published AutoDNA in Nature, using a multi-agent architecture to turn a natural-language request into 20+ instrument types and 11,382 hardware operations, matching expert-level results in DNA data storage and clinical sample testing; USTC open-sourced the RNA foundation model structRFM in Nature the same week. 1. AI for Science: an AI-native lab runs a full biomolecular workflow end to end. AutoDNA lands in Nature: one sentence drives 20+ instrument types. On November 4, 2026, a Shanghai Jiao Tong University team and collaborators published An AI-native experimental laboratory for autonomous biomolecular operations in Nature, introducing AutoDNA. The architectural difference from earlier 'bolt-on' autonomous labs is decisive: AutoDNA uses multiple agents under a central Planner that coordinates specialists for literature search, reagent management, protocol design, code generation, hardware control, and hypothesis generation. Given a natural-language request, the system autonomously runs the full loop from literature search and reagent selection through experiment design, code generation, hardware execution, and result analysis. Two engineering pillars: a hardware abstraction layer and a digital twin. The system parses instrument manuals and abstracts device capabilities into natural-language 'atomic services' (a pipette, for example, becomes transfer and mix), after which a code agent generates control code and self-corrects. As a result, AutoDNA coordinates more than 20 instrument types and executes over 11,000 hardware operations at micron-level positioning and microliter-level liquid handling. Before execution, the system rehearses generated instrument code in a simulated environment, tracking liquid volumes and checking positions and settings; in one run, the simulation caught code attempting to read fluorescence before the sample container had been loaded, blocking the error ahead of costly real-world execution. Four representative applications, with checkable numbers. In nucleic-acid testing, the system ran a commercial fluorescent isothermal kit to detect African swine fever virus. In enzymatic de novo DNA synthesis, AutoDNA optimized two competing objectives, yield and time, without a human-defined search space, reaching 97.8% average per-step synthesis yield, comparable to published expert-optimized results, while cutting concurrent workflow execution time to roughly one third. In DNA data storage, the system synthesized and sequenced 78 DNA strands, ran for about 203.5 hours across 11,382 hardware operations, and exactly restored the original digital content. In cancer detection, given a preprocessed colorectal tumor sample with unknown sequence information, it autonomously completed five stages, sequencing, mutation identification, primer design, primer synthesis, and assay validation, identifying a KRAS G13D mutation and validating it with self-synthesized primers. The limits are worth recording too. In an accompanying commentary, James Zou, associate professor of biomedical data science at Stanford University, notes that task selection and physical platform configuration remain human work, and that long runs still require reagent replenishment and waste cleanup. Of 14 hardware errors recorded during AutoDNA runs, 8 were recovered automatically and 6 required human intervention; LLM stochasticity can also affect protocol reproducibility. The team plans stronger instruments, mobile robots that can transport reagents autonomously, and retrieval-augmented literature access. For AI×HPC teams, the value here is not 'unmanned' operation but a working engineering loop, build a rehearsal layer and graded error handling before 'unmanned' labs. AutoDNA's credibility comes from two things: pre-execution digital-twin rehearsal, and splitting 14 hardware errors into 8 auto-recovered and 6 requiring humans. Sources: AutoDNA lands in Nature (36Kr, Nov 5); Paper (Nature) (nature.com). The rest of the weekly watch covers South Korea's Hangang supercomputer, China Mobile AI infrastructure, the StarMind space AI computer, and Inkling 2 Small open weights.
